beginner: Brussels sprouts like rich, fertile soil with plenty of compost worked in, and they do best in firm, settled ground rather than loose, fluffy soil. Loose soil tends to give loose, open sprouts, so firm the bed before planting and keep it evenly moist but never waterlogged.
seasoned: Brussels sprouts are heavy feeders that reward a fertile, well-drained loam high in organic matter, but they have one quirk worth honoring: they sprout most tightly in firm, settled soil. Loose, recently dug ground encourages loose, blowy sprouts and lodging of the tall, top-heavy stalk, so work in compost ahead of time and let the bed firm up before planting. Keep moisture even through the long season; the plant needs steady water but resents waterlogged ground.

beginner: Brussels sprouts grow best in soil that is slightly acidic to neutral, about 6.0 to 7.0. A simple soil test tells you where you stand. If you have had clubroot, keeping the soil closer to neutral helps hold it back.
seasoned: Aim for a soil pH of about 6.0 to 7.0; the plant still does fine across a wider 5.5 to 7.5 band. Clubroot, the key brassica soil disease, is far more likely below pH 6.5, so where it is a concern hold the soil toward the neutral end and lime acidic ground well ahead of planting.

beginner: Brussels sprouts grow for a long time and need regular feeding. Mix a balanced fertilizer into the soil before planting, then feed with a nitrogen fertilizer about a month and again two months after planting. Once the little sprouts start forming, go easier on the nitrogen, because too much makes loose, leafy sprouts and brings aphids.
seasoned: Brussels sprouts are long-season heavy feeders that need steady nitrogen to build the tall, leafy stalk that carries the crop. Work a balanced fertilizer such as 10-10-10 into the bed before planting, then side-dress with nitrogen about 4 and 8 weeks after transplanting. Ease off heavy nitrogen once sprouts begin forming, since late, lush growth encourages loose, leafy sprouts and draws aphids.

beginner: Time to feed your brussels sprouts.
seasoned: Time to side-dress your brussels sprouts with nitrogen.

beginner: Use a balanced fertilizer like 10-10-10 at planting, then a nitrogen feed a month or two later.
seasoned: High N to build the stalk and leaves; a 10-10-10 starter worked in before planting, then a nitrogen side-dress such as 21-0-0 at about 4 and 8 weeks. Ease off N as sprouts set.

beginner: Follow the label rate for a nitrogen-rich vegetable fertilizer, applied beside the plants.
seasoned: Side-dress about half a cup of 21-0-0 per 10 feet of row at roughly 4 and 8 weeks after transplanting, watered in alongside the plants.

beginner: Brussels sprouts do well next to aromatic herbs, onions, and quick cool-season crops you can tuck in while the plants are small. The most important rule is to keep them away from other cabbage-family plants, which share the same pests and diseases.
seasoned: Most brussels sprouts companion pairings are traditional rather than trial-tested. The ones worth acting on are practical: aromatic herbs and alliums as scent-based deterrents for cabbage pests, small flowering plants such as sweet alyssum and dill to draw the parasitic wasps and hoverflies that attack aphids and caterpillars (a habitat tactic Clemson recommends for cole crops), and quick crops like lettuce that use the open ground while the slow brussels plants fill in. The well-grounded caution is to separate brussels sprouts from other brassicas, which share clubroot and the whole cabbage-family pest complex, a rotation and disease principle more than a tested adjacency effect.

beginner: Sweet alyssum makes lots of tiny flowers that bring in helpful insects which eat aphids, a major brussels pest.
seasoned: Sweet alyssum is one of the better-supported brussels companions because aphids are this crop's signature pest. Its low mats of tiny flowers are a classic insectary plant, drawing the hoverflies, lacewings, and parasitic wasps that prey on cabbage aphids and caterpillars, and Clemson specifically advises small flowers like alyssum near cole crops for biological control. Let it self-sow along the bed edge.

beginner: Dill's flowers attract helpful insects that hunt the aphids and caterpillars that bother brussels sprouts.
seasoned: Dill works for brussels sprouts mainly through beneficial insects. Its umbel flowers draw the parasitoid wasps and hoverflies that attack cabbage aphids and the cabbage-family caterpillars, and Clemson lists dill among the flowers to plant near cole crops for natural control. Let some flower, and keep it off to the side so it does not crowd the big plants.

beginner: Onions are a traditional neighbor for cabbage-family plants; their strong smell is said to help confuse and deter cabbage pests.
seasoned: Alliums are a traditional brassica companion, their pungent scent thought to mask the crop from the cabbage pests that hunt partly by smell. Shallow-rooted and undemanding, onions tuck around young brussels plants without competing for much. Treat it as a low-risk, scent-based aid rather than a proven control.

beginner: Keep brussels sprouts away from other cabbage-family plants like broccoli, cabbage, kale, and cauliflower. They share the same pests and diseases, so grouping them makes problems worse.
seasoned: Planting brussels sprouts shoulder to shoulder with their brassica relatives, broccoli, cabbage, cauliflower, kale, collards, concentrates the family's shared pests (cabbage aphids, cabbageworms, loopers, harlequin bugs, root maggots) and shared diseases in one spot, and repeated same-family planting lets soil-borne clubroot build up. Spread brassicas out and rotate where they grow each year.

beginner: You'll see clusters of small gray-green insects with a dusty, waxy coating on the new growth and, worst of all, packed down inside the developing sprouts where they are very hard to wash out. Leaves may curl and there can be a sticky film.
seasoned: The gray-green, waxy-coated cabbage aphid is the signature brussels sprouts pest. Colonies build on growing tips and leaf undersides and then lodge deep inside the developing sprouts, where they contaminate the marketable buds with insects and honeydew and are extremely hard to clean at harvest. Populations explode on the long-season late-summer and fall crop.

beginner: Cabbage aphids are tiny insects that suck the plant's juices and breed fast, especially on the long-season fall crop. They love brussels sprouts and hide right inside the little sprouts, which is the part you eat.
seasoned: Brevicoryne brassicae, a brassica-specialist aphid, sucks sap and reproduces rapidly; on brussels sprouts it feeds in the upper leaves, flower buds, and especially within the forming sprouts. Contamination of the harvested sprouts with aphids and sticky honeydew is usually the real problem rather than plant stunting.

beginner: Knock colonies off with a strong spray of water and hit the undersides of leaves and into the sprouts with insecticidal soap or neem oil, repeating every few days. Welcome ladybugs and lacewings, which eat aphids.
seasoned: Dislodge colonies with a strong jet of water and spray insecticidal soap, neem, or horticultural oil with thorough coverage of leaf undersides and into the sprouts; repeat every few days. Conserve natural enemies (the parasitoid Diaeretiella rapae, hoverflies, ladybugs) that suppress this aphid.

beginner: Check the growing tips and sprouts often and act early, before the aphids get down into the sprouts. Go easy on nitrogen fertilizer once sprouts form, since soft growth draws them, and clear away old cabbage-family plants after harvest.
seasoned: Scout growing tips and the leaf axils weekly and catch infestations before aphids colonize the sprouts. Avoid excess nitrogen once sprouts set (soft growth favors them), use reflective mulch or row cover on young plants, and destroy crop debris that carries them over.

beginner: You'll see ragged holes chewed in the leaves, green caterpillars on the plant, and dark droppings, and later the caterpillars may bore into the sprouts. Some loop up in the middle as they crawl.
seasoned: Ragged holes chewed in the leaves with green caterpillars and dark frass; as the season goes on, larvae also bore into the sprouts and foul them. Imported cabbageworms are velvety green; cabbage loopers move in a looping arch; diamondback larvae are small and wriggle when disturbed; the cross-striped cabbageworm shows black and white bands.

beginner: These are caterpillars that hatch from eggs laid by white butterflies and small moths. They love cabbage-family plants and chew the leaves, and they can tunnel into the sprouts you want to eat.
seasoned: The larvae of the imported cabbageworm, cabbage looper, and diamondback moth (Clemson rates the diamondback the most numerous in home gardens) feed on brassica foliage and contaminate the sprouts; the adults are white or brownish butterflies and moths that lay eggs on the leaves.

beginner: Spray Bt, which is safe and targets only caterpillars, or spinosad, and pick caterpillars and eggs off by hand from under the leaves. Spray again after rain, since it washes off.
seasoned: Spray Bt (Bacillus thuringiensis kurstaki) or spinosad, which target caterpillars and spare beneficials, and hand-pick larvae and eggs from leaf undersides. Repeat after rain, since Bt breaks down.

beginner: Cover plants with a light fabric row cover after planting to keep the butterflies and moths from laying eggs, clear away old cabbage-family plants, and watch for the first white butterflies as your signal to act.
seasoned: Use floating row cover or fine mesh from transplanting to exclude the egg-laying adults, clean up brassica debris that shelters pupae, and scout for the first white butterflies as a spray cue. Tighten control once sprouts begin forming, since damage to the buds is the costly kind.

beginner: Shield-shaped black-and-orange (or black-and-red) bugs on the leaves, which develop white or yellow spots, then brown and look tattered. It is mostly a warm-region problem and loves cabbage-family plants.
seasoned: Shield-shaped bugs up to about 3/8 inch, brightly black-and-yellow or black-and-red, feeding with piercing-sucking mouthparts that leave white stipples; affected leaves brown and look tattered, and heavy feeding wilts and deforms plants. A warm-region brassica specialist.

beginner: The harlequin bug is a colorful stink-bug relative that pierces the leaves and sucks the juices, leaving pale blotches. It strongly prefers cabbage-family plants, especially in the South.
seasoned: The harlequin bug (Murgantia histrionica) is a true bug that specializes on cole crops, most damaging in the southern United States, where it completes two to three generations a year and overwinters as an adult in debris and weeds.

beginner: Search out and crush the bugs, their barrel-shaped eggs laid in rows, and the young ones by hand. Use a row cover to keep them off, pull badly infested plants, and clear away weeds and old plants where they hide over winter.
seasoned: Hand-pick and crush adults, nymphs, and the barrel-shaped egg rows; exclude with floating row cover; remove heavily infested plants. Insecticidal soap, pyrethrum, or neem help where pressure is severe.

beginner: Clean up garden debris and cabbage-family weeds where the adults overwinter, use row cover, and consider a trap crop of cleome or mustard to lure them away from the main crop, then destroy it.
seasoned: Eliminate overwintering sites by removing crop debris and crucifer weeds, use row cover, and deploy an early trap crop of cleome or mustard to divert overwintering adults, then destroy it before the main crop is set out.

beginner: Lots of tiny round holes in the leaves of young plants, made by small dark beetles that jump away like fleas when you get close. Bad damage can stunt seedlings.
seasoned: Tiny round shot-hole pits chewed in the leaves of young plants; the small dark beetles jump like fleas when disturbed. Heavy feeding stunts or kills seedlings and slows establishment of the long-season crop.

beginner: Flea beetles are small jumping beetles that chew on young cabbage-family leaves. They hurt seedlings most, because a tiny plant can't grow fast enough to recover.
seasoned: Flea beetles chew the foliage of young brassicas and are most damaging at the seedling stage; a vigorous transplant generally outgrows them, but a stalled seedling can be set back badly.

beginner: Cover young plants with a row cover, and if there are a lot of beetles, use a spray such as spinosad. The main goal is to get the seedlings big enough to handle the damage.
seasoned: Protect seedlings with row cover and spray spinosad if pressure is high; the goal is getting plants past the vulnerable seedling stage.

beginner: Cover seedlings with row cover from the start, keep them strong with steady water and food so they grow past the damage, and pull nearby weeds in the cabbage family.
seasoned: Use row cover from transplanting, keep seedlings vigorous with even water and feeding so they grow through the damage, and clean up weedy brassica relatives nearby.

beginner: New transplants wilt and grow badly or fall over. If you pull one up, you'll find small white maggots eating the roots. It is worst in cool, wet soil.
seasoned: Transplants wilt, grow poorly, and may collapse; pulling a plant reveals small white maggots tunneling in the roots and lower stem. Damage is worst in cool, wet soil at establishment.

beginner: A small fly lays eggs at the base of the plant, and the maggots that hatch burrow down and eat the roots. The fly is most active in cool, damp weather.
seasoned: The larvae of the cabbage root fly tunnel into brassica roots; the adult lays eggs at the stem base, and the maggots feed below, sometimes killing young plants.

beginner: Once the maggots are in the roots you can't save that plant, so pull and throw away the badly damaged ones. Put your effort into protecting the rest from new eggs.
seasoned: There is no effective rescue once maggots are in the roots; remove and destroy badly affected plants and protect the rest from further egg-laying.

beginner: Put a small collar or disk around the base of each transplant to stop the fly from laying eggs there, or use a row cover. Avoid planting into cold, soggy soil, and rotate away from where cabbage-family plants grew.
seasoned: Place a collar or disk around the stem base at transplanting to block egg-laying, or use row cover; avoid planting into cold, wet soil and rotate away from where brassicas grew.

beginner: Plants wilt in the afternoon, stay small and yellowish, and don't bounce back. If you dig one up, the roots are swollen into lumpy, club-shaped knobs.
seasoned: Plants wilt in the heat of the day, grow stunted and yellowed, and recover poorly; roots are swollen into distorted clubs and galls instead of normal fine roots.

beginner: A germ that lives in the soil infects the roots of cabbage-family plants and makes them swell, which stops the plant from taking up water and food. It stays in the soil for years.
seasoned: A soilborne organism (Plasmodiophora brassicae) infects brassica roots and forms the galls, which block water and nutrient uptake. It persists in soil for many years, spreads in contaminated soil and water, and infects most readily in acidic soils below pH 6.5.

beginner: There's no cure once a plant has it, so pull and destroy infected plants. Keeping the soil from being too acidic (closer to neutral) helps hold it back, and growing cabbage-family plants only rarely in that spot starves the germ out.
seasoned: There is no cure once plants are infected; remove and destroy them. Raising soil pH toward neutral with lime suppresses the disease, and long rotations starve it out over time.

beginner: Don't grow brussels sprouts or other cabbage-family plants in the same spot more than once every few years, longer if you've had clubroot. Keep the soil from being too acidic, improve drainage, and clean soil off your tools.
seasoned: Rotate brassicas out of affected ground on a long cycle (UMN advises 5 to 7 years where clubroot is known), keep soil pH up, improve drainage, and avoid moving infested soil on tools and boots.

beginner: Yellow patches shaped like the letter V appear at the leaf edges, pointing inward, with black veins inside them. It can spread through the plant and rot the leaves and sprouts.
seasoned: Yellow, V-shaped lesions spread inward from the leaf margins, with the veins inside the V turning black; the disease moves through the vascular system and can blacken and rot foliage and sprouts.

beginner: A bacteria that often comes in on infected seeds or transplants. It gets into the leaves and travels through the plant's veins, spreading fastest in warm, wet weather.
seasoned: A seedborne bacterium (Xanthomonas campestris pv. campestris) that enters through leaf pores and wounds and moves through the veins; it spreads in warm, wet conditions and on infected seed or transplants.

beginner: There's no real cure, so remove and destroy infected plants to keep it from spreading. Don't handle or brush against the plants while they're wet, because that spreads the bacteria.
seasoned: There is no effective cure; remove and destroy infected plants. Avoid working among plants when foliage is wet, since that moves the bacteria.

beginner: Begin with clean, certified seed and healthy transplants, don't plant where cabbage-family crops grew recently, space plants for good airflow, and avoid overhead watering.
seasoned: Start with clean, certified seed and healthy transplants (a hot-water seed treatment helps), rotate 2 to 3 years away from brassicas, give plants room for airflow, and avoid overhead watering and handling wet foliage.

beginner: Small dark spots on the leaves that grow into round patches with rings inside them, like a tiny target. Bad cases yellow the leaves and can spot the sprouts.
seasoned: Dark lesions enlarge into circular spots with characteristic concentric rings (a target-spot look) and a yellow halo; severe spotting downgrades the leaves and can blemish the sprouts. Favored by warm, wet conditions.

beginner: A fungus that spreads in warm, wet weather and infects the leaves, leaving target-like spots. It is worse on crowded, damp plantings and can come in on infected seed.
seasoned: Fungi in the genus Alternaria (chiefly A. brassicicola) infect brassica foliage, spreading by spores in wind and splashing water; infected seed, crop debris, and long leaf wetness drive it.

beginner: Remove and destroy badly spotted leaves, improve airflow so leaves dry quickly, and use a copper spray if it spreads. Avoid wetting the leaves when you water.
seasoned: Remove and destroy spotted leaves and debris, improve airflow, avoid overhead watering, and apply a copper-based fungicide if pressure is high.

beginner: Start with clean seed, rotate away from brassicas, space plants for airflow, water at the soil line, and clear away old plant debris.
seasoned: Use clean, disease-free seed (a hot-water treatment helps), rotate about 3 years away from brassicas, space for airflow, water at the soil line, and clear crop debris that harbors spores.

beginner: Pale yellow blotches on top of the leaves, with fuzzy grayish growth on the underside, mostly in cool, damp weather. Bad cases discolor the leaves and can spot the sprouts.
seasoned: Pale yellow patches form on the upper leaf surface with a fuzzy gray growth underneath, mainly in cool, damp weather; severe infection discolors leaves and can blemish the sprouts. Brussels sprouts' cool, humid season overlaps the weather it likes.

beginner: A mold-like disease that loves cool, wet, humid weather and spreads through the air and water. Wet leaves and crowded plants make it worse.
seasoned: A fungus-like organism (Hyaloperonospora brassicae) that thrives in cool, wet, humid conditions and spreads by spores in water and air; long leaf wetness and crowded plantings favor it.

beginner: Open up the airflow so leaves can dry, remove the worst leaves, and use a copper spray if it's spreading. It's hard to stop once the weather stays damp.
seasoned: Improve airflow and let foliage dry, remove badly affected leaves, and apply a copper-based fungicide if pressure is high; the disease is hard to stop once humidity stays high.

beginner: Space plants so air moves between them, water at the soil instead of from above, and pick resistant varieties if downy mildew is common where you live.
seasoned: Space plants for good air movement, water at the soil line rather than overhead, and choose resistant varieties where downy mildew is common.

beginner: Water regularly so the soil stays evenly moist, roughly 1 to 1.5 inches a week.
seasoned: Give about 1 to 1.5 inches weekly, kept even through the long season.

beginner: Aim for roughly 1 to 1.5 inches of water a week.
seasoned: About 1 to 1.5 inches per week, a little more in hot, dry spells while the plant is sizing up.

beginner: Water at the base of the plant rather than over the leaves.
seasoned: Water at the soil line with drip or a soaker hose where possible.

beginner: Lower leaves yellow and the plant looks soggy and limp.
seasoned: Yellowing lower leaves and limp growth; brussels sprouts dislike waterlogged soil and can rot at the crown or fall prey to root maggots in cold, wet ground.

beginner: Wilting leaves and small, loose, bitter sprouts.
seasoned: Wilting, stalled growth, and loose, bitter sprouts; drought stress during sprout formation directly hurts sprout quality.

beginner: Keep the soil or tray damp while the seeds come up, without letting the surface dry out.
seasoned: Keep the seedbed or tray surface evenly moist through germination; brassica seed is shallow and should not dry mid-emergence.

beginner: Keep the young plants evenly damp as they grow.
seasoned: Grow the seedlings on with steady, even moisture.

beginner: Keep the soil evenly damp while the tall plant grows over the long season. A strong leafy stalk now means more sprouts later.
seasoned: Even moisture matters most while the plant builds its tall frame over the long season; a strong stalk of leaves now supports the sprouts later.

beginner: As the little sprouts form up the stem, keep watering evenly. Dry spells now make small or loose sprouts.
seasoned: As sprouts form and fill up the stalk, keep steady even moisture; drought now gives small, loose, or bitter sprouts.

beginner: Keep watering evenly and pick sprouts from the bottom of the stalk up as they get firm. They taste sweeter after a frost.
seasoned: Keep even moisture and pick sprouts from the bottom up as they firm; flavor sweetens after frost.

beginner: Keep the water steady so the plant grows without stalling and the sprouts stay firm.
seasoned: Even moisture across the long season keeps the plant growing steadily and the sprouts firm; dry spells stall the plant and give loose, bitter sprouts.

beginner: Water steadily while the plant is growing big and while the sprouts are forming.
seasoned: Even moisture matters most while the plant is building its frame and again as the sprouts form and fill.

beginner: Brussels sprouts take a long time to grow, so it is easiest to start them as transplants. Sow seeds indoors about 5 to 6 weeks before you plant out. In cold areas, plant out in late spring or early summer so they mature in fall. In warm areas, plant in late summer or fall for a winter crop. Let homegrown seedlings get used to the outdoors over a week before planting.
seasoned: Brussels sprouts are almost always transplanted because of their long season. Start seeds indoors about 5 to 6 weeks before set-out. In cold regions, sow in spring and transplant in late spring or early summer to mature in the cool fall; in warm regions, sow in mid to late summer and transplant in late summer or fall for a winter crop. Set out sturdy young plants with about 4 to 6 true leaves and harden them off over 7 to 10 days.

beginner: A good-quality potting mix, not garden soil.
seasoned: A rich, well-drained commercial potting mix high in organic matter.
render_status_label: C -- never referenced in either app repo

beginner: Mix in compost and a slow-release fertilizer for the long season.
seasoned: Blend in compost and a slow-release balanced fertilizer; container plants feed for months and exhaust a small soil volume.

beginner: Pots dry out faster than the ground, so check daily in warm weather; a tall plant in a pot is thirsty.
seasoned: Containers dry faster than beds; check moisture daily in heat and water before the mix dries, since drought stress loosens the sprouts.
render_status_label: C -- never referenced in either app repo

beginner: Feed a bit more often than in the ground, since watering washes nutrients out of pots.
seasoned: Container plants need more frequent feeding than in-ground ones because watering leaches nutrients over the long season.

beginner: In mild-winter areas, a brussels plant in a big pot keeps standing and producing through the cold; just move it to a sheltered, sunny spot and keep picking. In cold areas, the small soil volume freezes hard, so pull the pot against the house during deep freezes or harvest the whole stalk before the worst cold.
seasoned: Brussels sprouts are cold-hardy enough to stand through winter in a container in mild zones, holding their sprouts in a sheltered, sunny spot. In colder zones the limited root volume freezes harder than open ground, so move containers against a wall during hard freezes, or treat the potted crop as a single fall-into-early-winter planting and cut the stalk before deep cold.

beginner: Brussels sprouts can grow in a large pot, but they are tall, top-heavy, long-season plants, so they are not the easiest container crop. Use a deep pot of at least 5 gallons, one plant per pot, stake it so it does not topple, and keep it well watered and fed. Pick sprouts from the bottom up.
seasoned: Brussels sprouts are a marginal container crop: they are large, top-heavy, and occupy the pot for months, so the gains of a container (mobility, soil control) come with real demands. Use a deep, heavy container of at least 5 gallons (10 is better), one plant per pot, stake the stalk against toppling, and keep moisture and feeding steady since a small soil volume runs out over a long season. The general container-vegetable guidance applies; brussels-specific container figures are modeled, not separately sourced.

beginner: A self-watering pot is a good match because it keeps the water steady, which the long-season plant needs.
seasoned: A self-watering container suits brussels sprouts well, since it smooths out the steady moisture that keeps the plant growing and the sprouts firm over a long season.

beginner: Brussels sprouts get tall and top-heavy, so give one plant a deep, heavy pot that holds at least 5 gallons and is about 12 inches deep, and stake it so it does not tip over. A wide, sturdy pot is better than a tall skinny one.
seasoned: Brussels sprouts grow into a tall, top-heavy stalk with a substantial root system, so choose a deep, wide-based container of at least 5 gallons and 12 inches deep for stability, and stake the plant. A broad, heavy pot resists toppling and buffers the fast drying a narrow pot suffers.

beginner: Jade Cross and Long Island Improved are easy, dependable choices, and Long Island Improved lets you save seed. Diablo is a later, heavy producer for a long cool season. Hestia gives neat, even sprouts, and red types like Redarling are pretty but slower. If brassica diseases are a problem where you live, look for a disease-resistant variety such as Nautic.
seasoned: Match the variety to the season length. Where the season is short, lean on early types (Jade Cross, Long Island Improved) that finish before deep cold; where it is long and cool, late heavy-yielders like Diablo reward the wait. Hybrids (Jade Cross, Hestia, Nautic, Diablo) give more uniform sprouts and firmer standing than the open-pollinated Long Island Improved, which in turn is the one to grow for saving seed. Where brassica disease is chronic, choose a resistant hybrid such as Nautic. Red types are slower and more ornamental than productive.

beginner: Other cabbage-family crops like broccoli, cabbage, cauliflower, kale, and turnips.
seasoned: Other brassicas (broccoli, cabbage, cauliflower, kale, collards, kohlrabi, turnip, radish, mustard), which share clubroot and the cabbage-family pests.

beginner: Don't plant brussels sprouts or other cabbage-family crops in the same spot year after year. Waiting at least 3 years between them, and longer if you have had clubroot, helps avoid soil diseases.
seasoned: Rotate so brussels sprouts and their brassica relatives do not return to the same ground for at least 3 years, and longer where clubroot is present; the University of Minnesota advises against growing cole crops where they grew in the past four years, and clubroot warrants a 5-to-7-year break. Holding soil pH near neutral also helps suppress clubroot.

beginner: Don't leave brussels sprouts out on the counter; they soften and yellow fast. Refrigerate them soon after picking, and remember the plant keeps them best of all, holding the sprouts on the stalk in cold weather.
seasoned: Sprouts soften and yellow at room temperature within a day or two, so refrigerate promptly after picking. A key brussels advantage is that the plant itself is the best storage: sprouts hold firm on the standing stalk for weeks in cold weather, so harvest close to use.

beginner: Store brussels sprouts unwashed in a perforated bag in the fridge's crisper drawer, where they stay good for about 3 to 5 weeks. Keep them away from apples and other ripening fruit, which make them go off sooner.
seasoned: Refrigerate unwashed in a perforated bag in the crisper; sprouts hold their quality for roughly 3 to 5 weeks, and up to several months near 32°F at high humidity. Keep them away from ethylene-producing fruit, which yellows them faster.

beginner: Brussels sprouts freeze well if you blanch them first. Trim and wash them, boil 3 to 5 minutes, cool right away in ice water, drain, and freeze. They keep up to about a year.
seasoned: Brussels sprouts freeze well once blanched: trim and wash, blanch about 3 to 5 minutes depending on size, cool quickly in ice water, drain, and freeze. Blanching halts the enzymes that otherwise cause off-flavors and loss of color, and frozen sprouts keep up to about a year.

beginner: Brussels sprouts are best right after picking, and the plant is its own best storage: in cold weather the sprouts hold on the stalk for weeks and even get sweeter after frost. You can also cut the whole stalk and stand it in a cool spot. Pick what you need when you need it, and chill it quickly.
seasoned: Quality is highest straight from the garden, and the standing plant is its own cold store: a whole stalk can be cut and kept upright in a cool cellar, or left in the garden to harvest as needed while temperatures stay above about 20°F. The sprouts sweeten in the cold, so there is little reason to stockpile; chill promptly whatever you pick.

beginner: In about 5 to 10 days, your seeds sprout and push up their first two little leaves (the seed leaves).
seasoned: Seeds sprout in about 5 to 10 days, pushing up two seed leaves (cotyledons). Brussels sprouts are started indoors for transplanting because of their long season.

beginner: Keep the starting mix damp. Once the first real leaves appear, give the seedlings strong light so they do not get leggy.
seasoned: Keep the starting mix evenly moist and give bright light from emergence to avoid stretch; thin or pot up once the first true leaves appear.

beginner: Have your seeds come up yet?
seasoned: Did your brussels sprouts seeds sprout?

beginner: The seedlings grow their real leaves and a stronger stem. They are ready to plant out at about 5 to 6 weeks old, with several true leaves.
seasoned: Young plants build true leaves and a sturdy stem; transplants are ready at about 4 to 6 true leaves, roughly 5 to 6 weeks from sowing. Set out sturdy young plants rather than oversized ones.

beginner: Harden the seedlings off over about a week before planting out. Watch for flea beetle holes on the young leaves.
seasoned: Harden off over 7 to 10 days before setting out at the wider 18-to-24-inch spacing; protect seedlings from flea beetles and cabbage root maggot with row cover and collars.

beginner: How many real leaves do your seedlings have?
seasoned: Are your transplants ready to go out?

beginner: The plant grows into a tall, leafy stalk over the summer (in cool regions) or fall (in warm regions). This is when it builds the frame that will carry the sprouts.
seasoned: The plant builds a tall, leafy stalk over several weeks, laying down the frame whose leaf axils will later carry the sprouts. Steady growth now sets the yield; the stalk does not form sprouts until cool weather arrives.

beginner: Here is the trick: brussels sprouts need cool weather to form good sprouts, so plant them to mature in fall, not summer. Then pick from the bottom up as the sprouts firm, a few at a time, instead of waiting for the whole plant. Be patient, the best sprouts come after frost.

New growers often plant too late, pick too early (before the sprouts firm up and a frost sweetens them), or give up on a plant that simply has not reached cool weather yet.

beginner: You found dense clusters of small gray-green insects tucked down inside the sprouts, hard to wash out. Cabbage aphids love brussels sprouts and hide right in the sprouts, and they breed fastest on soft growth from too much nitrogen on the long fall crop. People often miss them until harvest. seasoned: Dense cabbage-aphid colonies lodged inside the sprouts, contaminating the harvested buds and very hard to clean. The waxy gray-green cabbage aphid specializes on brassicas, explodes on the long-season fall crop, and favors the soft growth excess nitrogen produces. Next time scout tips and axils weekly, dislodge colonies early with a water jet or insecticidal soap into the axils, taper nitrogen as sprouts set, and conserve natural enemies; once aphids are inside the sprouts they are nearly impossible to remove.

beginner: Your plants stayed small and yellowish, wilted in the afternoon, and when you dug one up the roots were swollen into lumps. That is clubroot, a soil disease that infects cabbage-family roots and lasts for years in the soil. It builds up when brassicas are grown in the same spot repeatedly and in acidic soil. Next time, rotate so cabbage-family crops do not return to that bed for several years, keep the soil pH near neutral, and improve drainage.
seasoned: Plants were stunted and chlorotic, wilted by day, and showed galled, clubbed roots, the signature of clubroot (Plasmodiophora brassicae). The soilborne organism persists for years and builds under repeated brassica cropping and acidic, poorly drained soil. Next time rotate cole crops out for at least 3 years (5 to 7 where clubroot is known), lime toward a neutral pH, and improve drainage; there is no in-season cure.

beginner: Rotate brassicas out of that bed for several years, keep soil pH near neutral, and improve drainage.
seasoned: Use a long brassica rotation, raise pH toward neutral, improve drainage, and remove and destroy infected plants.

beginner: In cold regions, brussels sprouts are a single long-season crop. Harvest progressively up the stalk from the first frosts, which sweeten the sprouts, into early winter while temperatures hold above about 20°F. In the milder z7 the harvest often runs into January.

beginner: Brussels sprouts grow as small cabbage-like buds along a tall stalk, and you pick them a few at a time from the bottom up. They take a long time, about 3 to 6 months, and taste best when they mature in cool fall weather. Frost makes them sweeter, so the best sprouts come after the cold sets in. Summer heat makes them loose and bitter, so they are really a fall and winter crop.
seasoned: Brussels sprouts are a cool-season brassica grown for the small, cabbage-like buds that form in the leaf axils along a tall central stalk, harvested progressively from the bottom up. A long-season crop needing roughly 90 to 180 days, it is timed to mature in cool fall and winter weather: heat gives loose, bitter sprouts, while frost actually sweetens them, so the best sprouts come after the first hard frosts. It is one of the most cold-hardy garden vegetables, standing in the garden into early winter while temperatures hold above about 20°F.

beginner: Start picking at the bottom of the stalk when the lowest sprouts are firm and about 1 inch across, like tiny cabbages, and still tight and green. Twist them off and pull the leaf under them, then work up the stalk over the following weeks. They taste sweetest after a frost.
seasoned: Pick sprouts from the bottom of the stalk upward once they are firm, tight, and about 1 to 1.5 inches across, deep green, before they loosen or yellow. Snap or twist off the lowest mature sprouts and strip the leaf below each as you go; the upper sprouts keep sizing up for weeks. Flavor is best after a frost or two.

beginner: Before planting, mix plenty of compost into a rich, well-drained bed and let it settle so it is firm rather than fluffy, which helps the sprouts grow tight. Try not to plant where you grew other cabbage-family crops in the last few years, since that spreads soil diseases.
seasoned: Work plenty of compost into a fertile, well-drained bed before planting and confirm pH is near 6.0 to 7.0. Then let the bed firm up: brussels sprouts set tighter sprouts in settled soil, and loose ground gives blowy sprouts and a lodging-prone stalk. Because clubroot and other brassica diseases build in the soil, choose a bed where no cole crop has grown for at least 3 years.

beginner: Brussels sprouts grow for a long time, so most gardeners plant just one crop and pick from it for weeks, rather than planting in batches. In mild areas with a long cool season you can stagger a couple of plantings a month apart. The key is to plant so the sprouts form in cool fall weather; in hot areas, skip summer and grow them for fall and winter.
seasoned: Brussels sprouts are largely a single long-season planting rather than a true succession crop: each plant holds the bed for months and is harvested progressively up the stalk. In short-season regions, set out one crop and let it ride. In long, mild regions such as the cool coast you can stagger a couple of sowings about a month apart to spread the harvest. Time plantings so the sprouts form in cool weather; in hot regions skip summer and plant for a fall and winter crop.
